bibliography.abstract: Cities need to anticipate where energy-price shocks could intensify hardship beyond established hotspots. How income distributions and fuel-price balances jointly shape this hidden exposure remains unclear. Here we address this gap by stress-testing nearly one million properties in six English local authorities, combining required-energy costs for existing housing with modelled local income distributions. Under gas-led crisis prices, 41% of neighbourhoods in the highest local exposure quarter lie outside the highest official fuel-poverty quarter. Electricity-led stress changes this hidden geography: when electricity unit prices alone triple from 2021, comparable to the unmitigated late-2022 cap increase, 38% of the resulting hidden-exposure group are absent from the crisis-based group. Entering neighbourhoods have newer, more efficient housing, more flats and greater electricity dependence than retained areas. Crisis preparedness should extend household protection beyond current hardship hotspots, using fuel-specific stress tests to anticipate support needs as fuel prices and heating systems change.
bibliography.title: Hidden urban exposure to energy-price shocks: spreading burdens and shifting hotspots

en.caveats: The analysis relies on modelled local income distributions and required energy usage estimates rather than observed household expenditure data.
en.what: By stress-testing required energy costs against modelled income distributions for nearly one million properties across six English local authorities, this study maps vulnerability under different price scenarios. Under gas-led crisis prices, 41% of neighbourhoods in the top quartile for exposure fall outside the highest official fuel-poverty quartile. In a scenario where electricity prices triple from 2021 levels, 38% of exposed neighbourhoods shift to areas with newer, more energy-efficient housing and higher proportions of flats.
en.why: It demonstrates that official fuel-poverty metrics miss significant vulnerability during price spikes, revealing that decarbonised heating transitions introduce novel exposure risks to households outside traditional hardship zones.
